lesson.title: When Evidence Isn't Enough: Belief Perseverance
lesson.summary: Belief perseverance is the tendency for people to cling to an original belief even after the evidence that first supported it has been completely discredited.
lesson.body:
Belief perseverance describes a stubborn feature of human reasoning: once a belief is formed, it can survive long after the information that created it has been shown to be false. This might sound like simple bias, but it is deeply connected to cognitive dissonance. Abandoning a belief we have already acted on, defended in conversation, or built part of our identity around creates the same kind of uncomfortable inconsistency that dissonance theory describes. Rather than sit with that discomfort, people frequently resolve it by holding onto the belief and finding reasons to dismiss or minimize the disconfirming evidence instead.

One well known line of research on this, conducted by Lee Ross, Mark Lepper, and colleagues in the mid-1970s, gave participants false feedback about their performance on a task, such as distinguishing real suicide notes from fabricated ones, and then fully explained to participants that the feedback had actually been randomly assigned and had nothing to do with their real ability. Even after this thorough debriefing, participants' self assessments of their own ability often remained skewed in the direction of the original, fake feedback. The belief, once formed, had a kind of momentum that the correction alone could not fully undo.

A related and often cited real world example comes from Festinger's own later work with Henry Riecken and Stanley Schachter, published as "When Prophecy Fails" in 1956, which described a small group that believed the world would end on a specific date. When the predicted date passed without incident, the group did not simply abandon its belief. Instead, some members intensified their commitment and began actively recruiting new followers, a pattern the researchers interpreted as a dissonance reduction strategy: since the failed prophecy could not be undone, gathering more social support for the belief helped offset the psychological cost of admitting they had been wrong.

It is worth being cautious here about how far to generalize. Popular discussion sometimes claims that correcting a false belief can actually backfire and strengthen it, but the research literature on this so called backfire effect is genuinely mixed, and more recent, larger studies have often failed to replicate strong backfire effects. What is well supported is the narrower claim that beliefs frequently persist well past the point where their original evidentiary basis has collapsed, not that corrections reliably make things worse. Belief perseverance also sets up the next concept directly: one of the main tools the mind uses to protect a belief from correction in the first place is to selectively seek out and favor information that supports it, which is exactly what confirmation bias describes.
